summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passage by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 and by the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force in the province.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than repeal. A national DNU of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care and is under litigation. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors; legal experts called it illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts, with the outcome not recorded in the sources available here.

The provincial Ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, documented in a submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review that provincial police, or third parties acting under police cover, committed violence, persecution and harassment against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province.

Trans and travesti women in the province face indirect criminalisation through drug-offence and street-offence prosecutions. After Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences in 2005, microtrafficking enforcement in La Plata's Zona Roja became the operative instrument of this practice, even though the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence.

In February 2025 the national government banned housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in women's prisons. This policy is national; Buenos Aires province has no trans-specific placement rule of its own, and no separate trans housing unit is recorded.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented high in 2025, with at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity recorded during the year, averaging one every 38 hours. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino's 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Agencia Presentes reported on 19 March 2026 that the 2025 hate-crime figures represent an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.
localsOnly:
The provincial Ombudsman published in September 2024 a guide to gender-marker rectification for people born in Buenos Aires province, setting out registry rectification steps and including provisions for people born in the province now living elsewhere. The guide documents provincial implementation of the recognition regime established by the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law.

Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences in 2005, the devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation of trans and travesti women, particularly in La Plata's Zona Roja.

The provincial Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, is the provincial body that documents and reports on gender-based violence, including its 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of litigation against the February 2025 decree on minors' gender-affirming care is not recorded in the sources available here and remains unresolved.

Whether the December 2024 DNU's consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors have been upheld, modified or struck down in that litigation is not sourced here.

No trans-specific prison placement rule for Buenos Aires province beyond the national February 2025 ban is sourced; whether the province operates any separate trans housing unit is unresolved in these materials.

Current enforcement patterns of the 2005 drug-jurisdiction practice against trans and travesti women in La Plata's Zona Roja are documented through academic sources of varying dates; recent provincial enforcement data is not sourced here.
